chunks: "For me, design for test is making sure I can both set up and see what's happening inside the board, for the factory and for me at the bench.
On the physical side, I'd give every power rail, ground, reset, clock, and key signal a test pad, with ground pads right next to them so a scope ground spring can reach.
I'd put a programming and debug connector on, SWD or JTAG, and a UART header, and leave a path for factory fixtures by putting pads on one side at a pitch the fixture supports.
I'd also build the board so I can partition it.

Zero-ohm links or jumpers in series with supplies, so I can power one block at a time or measure its current; a way to hold the processor in reset; and pull-up and pull-down options so strapping pins can be forced.
On the firmware side: a test mode, status LEDs, loopbacks on communication ports, and boundary scan on parts where I can't reach the pins, like BGAs. Then I trade it off.
Every test pad costs area and, on fast nets, a bit of capacitance, so I prioritise by risk, and for high-speed or sensitive signals I use a tiny stub or an in-line pad, or rely on built-in self-test.
And I check the plan with the factory's test engineer before layout is final."
